# Automation Tool Ideas — Roman 1:1, 2026-08-25

Hand-authored candidate list. Source: the "Aidan / Roman Meet & Greet" (Aug 25, 2026,
12:30 PM CDT) transcript, plus PressW process context.

**This file is not `candidates.md`.** That one is generated by `automation-spotter/` from
observed session behavior and should not be hand-edited. This is the complementary
top-down list: what the business says it needs, rather than what the transcripts show us
repeating. Where the two agree, confidence is high.

Nothing here is scoped, estimated, or committed. It is a menu.

## Framing from the conversation

Roman set four pillars in priority order: (1) client delivery, (2) R&D and automation,
(3) the process pipeline between strategy and engineering, (4) stop-gap strategy coverage
for three legacy clients. He named the core tension explicitly — all R&D and clients drop,
all delivery and the business only scales by hiring. Stated ideal end state: Roman and
Aidan alone servicing 100 clients through automation.

Quality model he described: skill factory gets a deliverable to 60–70%, the tuning agent
takes it to ~80%, the last mile closes through client feedback and lived examples. PressW
sells ~90% of the busy work removed, never a one-click end-to-end promise.

---

## A. Skill factory eval infrastructure

The R&D mandate Roman said needs attention "probably daily."

1. **Retro-benchmark harness** — re-run already-shipped client skills through the current
   skill factory and diff against what was actually delivered. Aidan proposed this in the
   call; Roman called it "100% valid" and said it should become a CI/CD step.
2. **Model-release regression gate** — before adopting a new model (Fable 6, Opus 6, …),
   replay the factory against the prior corpus and fail loudly on parity loss. Roman:
   if a new model with the skill factory can't recreate what the previous one did,
   "that's failure right there." He called the eval infrastructure "a must in any case."
3. **Gold-standard corpus manager** — a versioned store of (client input → accepted output)
   pairs harvested from past deliveries. Everything above depends on this existing. Roman
   noted "we do have a lot of gold standards" already, unorganized.
4. **Factory capability map** — automated classification of which deliverable types the
   factory actually reaches 60–70% on versus which are, in his words, "just not going to
   be skill-factorable necessarily." Built from eval results rather than intuition.
5. **Parallel-track runner** — the two-session pattern Roman described directly: deliver by
   hand in one Claude session while the factory attempts the same job in another, then diff
   and file the delta as factory improvements. His fallback if unautomated was blocking
   5–6pm daily to do it manually.

## B. Prose CI/CD — reviewing skills the way we review code

Roman's framing: "we're not reading fucking paragraphs of skills," and prose lacks the
input/output sanity checks code has.

6. **Skill contradiction linter** — detect the failure he named as already live on client
   skills: a ~50-step skill where an early step says do X and a later step says do the
   opposite, because different rounds of feedback were fitted into different sections.
7. **Overfit / drift detector** — flag when client-feedback tweaks have narrowed a skill
   past generalization, and surface which feedback round introduced each instruction.
   Roman: "we overfitted it too much because they keep sending us feedback."
8. **Prose diff reviewer** — a code-review equivalent for skill edits: what changed
   semantically, what it might break, which eval cases now cover it.
9. **Ship-blocker preflight** — cold-start validation from a clean client environment
   before handoff. Roman predicted this exact failure unprompted: a skill ships, was never
   run locally by its author, and breaks for the client on something rudimentary. He said
   it has happened multiple times.

## C. Ontology

Roman's analogy: financial deliverables are all variations of the same thing. The ontology
describes "hands" — what they are, what the fingers do — and mixins say this client's hands
also play the violin, that one's play guitar.

10. **Ontology extractor from delivered work** — mine shipped deliverables (CIMs, financial
    models, debt memos, deal screens) for shared skeleton versus client-specific mixin.
11. **Ontology coverage report** — which deliverable types are described, which are missing,
    which have only one client's variant and are therefore probably overfit.
12. **Mixin proposer** — given a new client's examples, propose an existing ontology base
    plus deltas instead of authoring from scratch.

## D. Build-time accelerators

13. **MCP factory** — Roman raised this directly, crediting a conversation with Zach
    Johnson: point it at API docs, get a FastMCP Python server, async, no human in the
    loop. He described the manual version as already nearly one-shottable today — Fable to
    plan, Opus to execute, walk away for an hour — and said the next step is making it an
    agent that runs async.
14. **Standards-enforcement layer** — the FastMCP-not-JS-SDK problem generalized: house
    conventions Claude silently violates unless told. It built him an entire MCP server on
    the JavaScript SDK. His words: "I should have an agent that knows that, or I should
    have rules that know that."
15. **Deliverable scaffolder from the ontology** — "I have to build a CIM" becomes "generate
    the CIM generator," so the human job starts at discerning what is different for this
    client rather than at a blank file.

## E. Pillar 3 — the strategy↔engineering interface

Roman: this process "doesn't exist" today, and building it runs in both directions.

16. **Ticket intake quality gate** — reject or flag tickets missing what engineering needs:
    dates, estimates, priority, gold standard, source call. He framed the engineering job
    as defining the interface, not doing strategy's work: "I need dates on the tickets."
17. **Call → ticket pipeline** — Fireflies/Granola transcript to drafted Linear tickets with
    acceptance criteria, so "everything has a ticket" doesn't cost hours. He was emphatic:
    change one line anywhere and he wants a ticket — "I will hunt you down."
18. **Capacity / underwater signal** — automatic surfacing when ticket load exceeds capacity,
    into Linear and Argos where Zach and clients already look. He explicitly said he will
    not babysit this and needs it flagged, and that clients check Argos to see real work.
19. **Estimate calibration** — actual-versus-estimated from Linear and Harvest history.
    Also supplies defensible ammunition for the timeline-stretching he described: strategy
    needs to sell the one-pointer as a three-pointer to buy engineering R&D time.

## F. The R&D flywheel

Roman's rule: every manual execution should yield a learning fed back into R&D.

20. **Manual-execution capture** — end-of-session prompt asking what was just done by hand,
    what the factory couldn't do, filed as an R&D ticket. His manual fallback was a daily
    calendar block; automating the capture is strictly better.
21. **Cross-client architectural search** — "where have we done a CIM review before?"
    answered at the architectural level without moving any client IP. He noted the
    guardrails already block copy-paste but the pattern remains askable, and that asking
    it naturally surfaces ontology candidates.
22. **Decision-log / PRD generator** — he named PRD consistency, client-shareability, and
    multiplayer editing as a specific gap: "how do we write the PRD, keeping it consistent,
    sharing with the client, making it multiplayer."

## G. Legacy-client leverage

Roman covers S3 Ventures, Capital Creek Partners, and Lori Capital. Cheap early contracts,
big firms, heavy referral and reference flow, and friendly enough to prototype against.
Aidan pairs on all of these; Roman leads the calls.

23. **Maintenance-mode watchdog** — health checks on shipped skills for these three, so
    maintenance doesn't quietly eat delivery time.
24. **Referral / reference tracker** — these accounts are paid for in referrals and
    references; nothing currently makes that returned value visible.

---

## Filters before any of this becomes a ticket

Both are Roman's, stated in the call:

- **Don't automate what a person can fix manually in five minutes at current scale.** With
  five clients and twenty tickets, go fix the tickets by hand. File the "eventually this
  should be an agent" ticket and move on.
- **Prefer whatever generates skill-factory signal soonest.** The near-term goal he set is
  to deliver as much real client work as possible *through* the factory, specifically so we
  learn where it performs and where it doesn't.

## Immediate

The retro-benchmark harness (#1) is the one Roman verbally pre-approved and tied to a
deadline. He suggested picking something simple and trying it just to confirm the factory
is operational, ahead of the agent factory meeting Wednesday at 4:30, and said to review
Liam's agent factory artifacts before then.
